personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Goyle is established as physically large, thuggish, and almost entirely non-verbal. His dominant traits are dimness (described as 'almost as stupid as he was mean'), brute physical menace, sycophantic laughter at Malfoy's insults, and a kind of passive, reflexive obedience to Malfoy. He rarely speaks independently; his contributions are grunts, sniggering, cracking knuckles, and flexing arms. He is greedy (falls for the sleeping-draught cakes), and described with consistent animal/gorilla imagery: 'gorilla-ish arms,' 'gorilla-like,' 'low grunt.' His 'voice' in the handful of book lines he does have is minimalist and dull. He also shows small flickers of separate will late in the series — in Deathly Hallows he has opinions and speaks several lines independently ('We 'ung back, Potter... We decided not to go'), and he casts an Avada Kedavra, showing he has absorbed real Dark Arts training under Voldemort's regime. Ron's comment that impersonating Goyle requires acting 'less intelligent' reinforces his stupidity as a defining and comedic trait.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Goyle's physical bulk, his near-silence, and his role as a laughing presence at Malfoy's side. He sniggering at Malfoy's jokes, lumbers alongside him, and his few lines of dialogue are consistent with his dull, slow speech. In Deathly Hallows Part 2, the film gives Goyle the pivotal line 'C'mon, Draco. Don't be a prat. Just do 'im' and his use of Avada Kedavra and Fiendfyre are retained. His greedy swallowing of cakes is absent from the theatrical cut. His sycophantic reactions to Malfoy and his near-total silence across most films match the book baseline. One notable addition is that Blaise Zabini replaces Crabbe for much of the sixth and seventh films, which slightly dilutes the Goyle-specific presence, but what remains of Goyle's on-screen behaviour is faithful to type.
personality_voice.difference: The films largely preserve Goyle's surface personality — thuggishness, near-silence, sycophancy, physical menace. What is partially lost is the specific texture of that stupidity as rendered through narration (the book repeatedly emphasises his dimness through free indirect description and others' observations in ways the film cannot replicate). His late-series independent voice in Deathly Hallows — surprisingly speaking in full sentences, showing he has made a deliberate choice to stay behind and capture Harry — is present in the film, which is faithful. The cut Polyjuice preparation scene removes one small characterisation beat (greedily eating cakes without suspicion), but this is a minor loss. No traits are added that contradict the books.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality is preserved: dull, large, threatening, obedient to Malfoy, minimally verbal, capable of sycophantic laughter. The book's dense descriptive texture of his stupidity cannot transfer fully to film, but the observable behaviours that encode it largely do. A modest penalty is appropriate for the compression of this texture and the loss of a few minor greed/stupidity beats, but the character remains recognisable in all major traits. Score sits in the 14–17 range.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for most traits; reasonably inferred for the degree of loss from book narration.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Goyle's structural function is threefold: (1) physical intimidation and bodyguard alongside Crabbe for Malfoy; (2) a foil/comedic object whose stupidity is mined for humour; (3) a plot-functional role in Book 2 (his body is used for Polyjuice) and Books 6–7 (he acts as a lookout for Malfoy's Room of Requirement project and takes independent action in the Battle of Hogwarts). In Deathly Hallows he becomes briefly agentive: he decides independently to stay behind with Malfoy at Hogwarts rather than evacuate, he casts Avada Kedavra at Hermione (an act of genuine lethal aggression), and he sets off Fiendfyre, which kills him. These are the most plot-consequential things Goyle ever does and they are causally significant: the Fiendfyre destroys the diadem Horcrux and kills Goyle, driving the emotional beat of the scene. He also physically blocks Harry and serves as the main combat threat in the Room of Requirement.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the theatrical films, Goyle's bodyguard/intimidation function is preserved across multiple films. The Polyjuice plot in Chamber of Secrets loses the scene of Harry and Ron hiding and waking the real Crabbe and Goyle (cut), but the use of his body (hair) for the transformation is retained in context. In Half-Blood Prince and Deathly Hallows, Goyle appears as a lookout and then as a combatant. In Deathly Hallows Part 2, his 'Just do 'im' line, his Avada Kedavra, his triggering of Fiendfyre, and his death are all present. However, in the film it is Goyle (not Crabbe as in the book) who casts the Fiendfyre and dies, due to the recasting caused by Jamie Waylett's real-life legal issues. This transfer from Crabbe to Goyle is actually an increase in Goyle's agency relative to the books, not a decrease. His role as lookout in Book 6 is partially shown.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The primary agency-related loss is the cut Polyjuice scene (unconscious Crabbe and Goyle being dragged and stored), which removes a beat where Goyle's body is literally appropriated as a prop — a minor humiliation that adds texture. The transfer of Fiendfyre from Crabbe to Goyle in the films technically preserves the overall plot function and actually elevates Goyle's agency and narrative consequence. His role as Malfoy's lookout in Book 6 is present but compressed. The bodyguard intimidation function is consistent across both media.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Goyle's role and agency are largely preserved. The Crabbe-to-Goyle transfer in Deathly Hallows means Goyle's film role is, if anything, slightly elevated in consequence. The cut Polyjuice staging scene is a minor loss. No major action of Goyle's is given to another character — the Fiendfyre transfer goes to Goyle from Crabbe, not away from Goyle. A moderate score is appropriate: role and agency are recognisable and mostly intact, with some compression, scoring in the 10–13 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Goyle has almost no explicitly stated motivations in the books. His behaviour is entirely conditioned by: (1) following Malfoy's lead without question through most of the series; (2) implicit pure-blood supremacist ideology absorbed from his Death Eater father (his father is named as a Death Eater at the graveyard in Goblet of Fire); (3) in Deathly Hallows, a nascent independent motivation emerges — he wants to be 'rewarded' by Voldemort and deliberately positions himself to capture Harry, speaking with the simplistic avarice of 'a small child promised a large bag of sweets.' There is no genuine internal conflict in the books; Goyle has no moment of doubt or moral struggle. His motivations are externally driven and unreflective.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films give almost no access to Goyle's motivations — consistent with the books. His Deathly Hallows dialogue ('We 'ung back, Potter. We decided not to go. Decided to bring you to 'im.') preserves the book's portrait of a simple, reward-seeking loyalty to Voldemort. The film does not invent motivations or complicate them beyond what the books establish.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: Almost no change. The books themselves provide very little motivational material for Goyle, and the films faithfully represent that thinness. The main gap is the absence of the book's explicit statement about his Death Eater father's influence and the slight dimming of the 'child promised sweets' characterisation in the film (it is implied rather than narrated), but neither constitutes a meaningful alteration of what motivations exist.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The motivations are thin in both books and films. What little exists is preserved. The confidence is Low because there is simply not much to evaluate. A modest penalty for the slight loss of the explicit 'father as Death Eater' motivation context, which the books provide and the films do not foreground for Goyle specifically. Score in 8–10 range.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Reasonably inferred; the corpus provides limited direct evidence of Goyle's inner life in either medium.

character_arc.book_baseline: Goyle has a flat arc for most of the series: he is Malfoy's silent, thuggish follower from Book 1 through Book 6. In Book 7, there is a micro-arc: he makes an independent choice (to stay at Hogwarts and capture Harry for Voldemort), demonstrates genuine Dark Arts capability (Avada Kedavra, Fiendfyre), and dies as a direct consequence of his own action. This is a minimal but real arc — from passive follower to independently agentive Death Eater-in-training who dies by his own magic. It is not a moral arc but a functional one: he becomes genuinely dangerous and pays with his life.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves this micro-arc faithfully. Goyle is a passive follower for most of the series, then in Deathly Hallows Part 2 he speaks independently, casts lethal spells, triggers Fiendfyre (with the Crabbe-to-Goyle transfer noted above), and dies. The arc endpoint — death by Fiendfyre he himself unleashed — is intact.
character_arc.difference: The arc is compressed (the Book 6 section where Goyle serves as Malfoy's lookout and is part of the Room of Requirement surveillance is less developed in the film), but the critical narrative beats — passive follower → briefly independent and dangerous → dead — are all present. The transfer from Crabbe to Goyle for the Fiendfyre beat actually strengthens Goyle's arc in the film relative to the books.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Arc is compressed but faithful. The key turning point (Deathly Hallows independent agency and death) is preserved. Minor compression in Book 6 beats. Score in 11–13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Goyle's primary relationship is with Malfoy: total, unthinking subordination and loyalty. He does whatever Malfoy does, laughs when Malfoy laughs, flexes muscles when Malfoy needs intimidation. There is no warmth or genuine friendship in the books — it is hierarchical follower-leader with Goyle as a near-object. His relationship with Crabbe is one of identical pairing — they are often indistinguishable, described as a unit. By Deathly Hallows, a small fracture appears: Goyle's independent decision-making (staying behind, casting lethal spells) suggests a shift toward self-directed loyalty to Voldemort rather than purely to Malfoy.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Malfoy-Goyle dynamic is preserved as hierarchical subordination throughout the films. The Crabbe-Goyle unit is partially disrupted in the later films by Blaise Zabini's presence, which dilutes the Goyle-Crabbe pairing but does not misrepresent Goyle's relationship with Malfoy. The Deathly Hallows dynamic where Goyle shows mild independence from Malfoy ('Just do 'im') while still orbiting him is present. The emotional flatness of the relationship — no affection, no genuine loyalty, just proximity and use — is preserved.
key_relationships.difference: The main loss is the Crabbe-Goyle unit being partially broken up across the later films by Zabini's substitution. This does reduce the specific texture of their identical-pair function. The Malfoy-Goyle dynamic's key quality (total subordination) is intact. The Deathly Hallows scene where Goyle pushes past Malfoy to act independently (in the Room of Requirement, he steps into the breach when Malfoy hesitates) is present in the film.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationship with Malfoy is substantially faithful. The Crabbe-Goyle pairing is partially diluted in later films. A small penalty for the loss of the specific unit-pairing texture. Score in 7–8 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Goyle is not a complex character, but the books give him specific texture that goes beyond generic thug: (1) his stupidity is carefully calibrated — Ron mimes writing as Goyle in Book 5 ('I must not look like a baboon's backside') as a specific comedy beat; (2) the Polyjuice sequence in Book 2 gives him unusual centrality — Harry literally inhabits his body, observes his appearance from the inside, and the narration generates specific physical detail (bristly hair, dull deep-set eyes, thick wrists, boatlike shoes, low rasp of voice); (3) his cowardice/fear under the Invisibility Cloak mud-attack in Book 3 (he hops in pain, tries to rub mud from his small dull eyes) shows vulnerability; (4) he attempts to steal leprechaun gold in Book 4 (Hagrid calls him out); (5) he genuinely attempts to harm Harry and Hermione with Avada Kedavra in Deathly Hallows — the most morally definitive act the books give him; (6) the description of Crabbe and Goyle at the Slytherin table after Malfoy's departure in Half-Blood Prince ('oddly lonely without the tall pale figure of Malfoy between them, bossing them around') is a rare moment of pathos.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve his physical presence and intimidation function. The Deathly Hallows combat scenes give him genuine menace. What is lost: (1) the Polyjuice interior-view of Goyle's body (the cut scene removes the most intimate characterisation of Goyle in the series); (2) the specific comedy beats (Ron's impression, the leprechaun gold, Scabbers biting his finger) are absent; (3) the brief pathos of the lonely Crabbe-Goyle image in HBP is not present; (4) the mud-throwing vulnerability sequence from PoA is condensed — Crabbe and Goyle's knees go out (film) rather than Goyle hopping and rubbing mud from his eyes (book), losing the specific physical comedy.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film retains Goyle's broad identity but loses most of the specific textural material that made him more than a generic thug: the Polyjuice intimate characterisation, the comedy beats, the pathos moment, and several small humiliation/vulnerability scenes. The films keep the functional outline but drop the detail. This is a noticeable simplification.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character is simplified but not unrecognisably so. The most significant single loss is the Polyjuice cut scene (excluded per instructions), which contained the richest characterisation of Goyle's physicality in the entire series. The remaining lost material (comedy beats, pathos moment, mud humiliation) cumulatively reduces the texture meaningfully. Score in 8–10 range.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for losses; reasonably inferred for cumulative effect.

score_caps_applied: Cap 4 considered (score above 70 only if films preserve more than broad identity): Films do preserve specific behaviours and key plot beats beyond broad identity — Deathly Hallows agency is faithfully rendered — so cap 4 does not strictly apply, but the cumulative texture loss from cut and absent scenes keeps the score naturally below 75.
comparative.key_observations: Goyle is a minor character whose book characterisation is already thin, so the films have relatively little to preserve or lose. The surface identity — large, dull, silent, thuggish, obedient to Malfoy — is consistently maintained across all films. The most significant faithfulness concern is the loss of the Polyjuice body-inhabitation sequence (cut from theatrical release per instructions), which contained the series' richest physical and comedic characterisation of Goyle. Several smaller comedy and humiliation beats from the books are absent. Conversely, the adaptation of the Deathly Hallows Room of Requirement scene is largely faithful, and the transfer of the Fiendfyre role from Crabbe to Goyle actually strengthens Goyle's narrative consequence in the film. The character scores moderately: the broad strokes are right, the specific texture is meaningfully reduced, and the confidence is Medium throughout due to the limited dialogue corpus available for Goyle in both media.
